chunks: Then He created (glorified is He) the opening of the atmosphere, the splitting of the firmament, and the strata of the winds,

He flowed into it water whose current was stormy and whose surges leapt one over the other. He loaded it upon the back of the dashing wind and the breaking typhoons, so He ordered them to shed it back, gave them control over its vigor, and acquainted them with its limit,
the wind blowing beneath it with force, and the water flowing above it with abundance.
Then He created (glorified is He) a wind whose direction was established, whose position was perpetuated, whose motion was intensified, and whose source was far-reaching,
so He ordered it to raise the deep water and stir the waves of the oceans,
so it churned it like the churning of a water-skin, and pushed it fiercely into the firmament,
returning its front to its rear, and its stationary parts to its flowing parts,
until its foam bubbled up, and its piled-up surface threw forth foam.
so He raised it into an opening air and a vast firmament,
and He fashioned from it seven heavens, making their lowest a restrained wave, their highest a protected ceiling, and their thickness elevated,
without pillars to support them, nor nails to hold them together.
Then He adorned them with the adornment of the stars and the light of the meteors,
and set in them a shining lamp and a luminous moon:
in a revolving orbit, a moving ceiling, and a rotating firmament.
ai.seo_question: How does Nahj al-Balagha describe the creation of the seven heavens and celestial bodies?
ai.summary: Imam Ali’s eloquent description aligns with the Shia exegetical tradition that views this passage as a profound reflection on the dynamic, non-static nature of creation, contrasting with the static 'firmament' of earlier cosmologies. It highlights the divine command (Amr) over natural forces like wind and water, illustrating the interconnectedness of the atmospheric and celestial realms as signs of God’s power. This narrative serves not only as cosmology but as a theological argument for the unity and order of the universe under a single Creator.
